{"id": "12:97/q05", "question": "For which wrongdoing do the sons ask forgiveness?", "turns_on": "Which people the sources identify as injured by the brothers' sins.", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q05/p1", "position": "Their treatment of Joseph.", "reasons": "MUQATIL identifies the wrongdoing as concerning Joseph; BIQAI calls it intentional wrongdoing against him. ISLAHI says the brothers confess to Jacob as they had confessed to Joseph at 12:91 after recognizing their folly."}, {"id": "12:97/q05/p2", "position": "The grief and injury they caused Jacob.", "reasons": "MAWARDI says they could answer for this only by honoring Jacob; JISHUMI identifies his grief; QURTUBI says his pardon alone could clear the injury."}, {"id": "12:97/q05/p3", "position": "Their wrongdoing against both Jacob and Joseph.", "reasons": "NASAFI names both the father and his son, along with the brothers' admission and repentance."}, {"id": "12:97/q05/p4", "position": "Their deeds against Joseph and Benjamin.", "reasons": "TABATABAI names both brothers and notes that Joseph had already forgiven them at 12:92."}, {"id": "12:97/q05/p5", "position": "Their deliberate sins against Jacob, Joseph, and Benjamin.", "reasons": "BURSEVI names all three and says the brothers also appeal to Jacob's compassion."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q06", "question": "When did Jacob seek forgiveness for his sons, and why did he delay?", "turns_on": "The transmitted timing differs among dawn, Friday, repeated Friday nights, and twenty years; other sources propose his hurt or a test of sincerity as the reason for delay.", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q06/p1", "position": "He waited until the night prayer or predawn, when prayer was unobstructed, and then prayed at dawn.", "reasons": "THALABI says most commentators specify predawn because prayer then is not veiled from God; he reports Jacob praying at dawn for his own grief and impatience over Joseph and for his sons' acts. MUHARIB IBN DITHAR reports Ibn Masud invoking forgiveness at dawn and citing Jacob's delay; DURR also transmits Ibn Masud's predawn account."}, {"id": "12:97/q06/p2", "position": "He delayed because he remained hurt, perhaps waiting until dawn or reconciliation, or signaling his grievance.", "reasons": "KURANYOLU presents these as possible explanations for his delay."}, {"id": "12:97/q06/p3", "position": "He waited until Friday.", "reasons": "THALABI transmits through Ikrima from Ibn Abbas a Prophetic explanation of Jacob's promise as waiting until Friday."}, {"id": "12:97/q06/p4", "position": "He sought forgiveness every Friday night for more than twenty years.", "reasons": "THALABI reports this from Wahb."}, {"id": "12:97/q06/p5", "position": "He waited until the predawn of Friday, which coincided with Ashura.", "reasons": "THALABI reports this from Tawus."}, {"id": "12:97/q06/p6", "position": "The brothers and Jacob sought forgiveness for twenty years before Gabriel taught Jacob a supplication and they received an answer.", "reasons": "IBNABIHATIM's report says their petitions for the treatment of Joseph were not accepted until Gabriel taught a prayer invoking God as the hope, aid, and helper of believers and beloved of penitents. MAWARDI transmits from al-Layth through Ibn Wahb the twenty years and Gabriel's teaching."}, {"id": "12:97/q06/p7", "position": "He delayed to test whether his sons were sincere and truthful.", "reasons": "STUDYQURAN reports this as a possible explanation for his delay."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q07", "question": "What do the reports say about the eventual forgiveness?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over when pardon was announced and whether its announcement included a covenant of future prophethood.", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q07/p1", "position": "At dawn, Jacob prayed for himself and his sons and God revealed that all were forgiven.", "reasons": "THALABI says Jacob included his own grief and impatience over Joseph and his sons' acts in the dawn prayer."}, {"id": "12:97/q07/p2", "position": "After twenty years of seeking pardon, Gabriel taught Jacob a supplication and their petition was answered.", "reasons": "IBNABIHATIM gives the supplication's appeals to God as believers' hope, aid, and helper and penitents' beloved. MAWARDI transmits the account from al-Layth through Ibn Wahb."}, {"id": "12:97/q07/p3", "position": "The brothers feared their parents' pardon was insufficient and requested God's pardon; twenty years later revelation announced forgiveness and a covenant of future prophethood among them.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL transmits this in a long report from Anas ibn Malik."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q08", "question": "What must a person who wrongs someone else do to obtain release?", "turns_on": "Whether the victim needs to know the nature and extent of the wrong to give meaningful pardon.", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q08/p1", "position": "The offender must ask the injured person for release and disclose the wrong and its extent.", "reasons": "QURTUBI applies this to wrongs to person or property and rejects a vague pardon because knowing the details could change the injured person's willingness to forgive."}, {"id": "12:97/q08/p2", "position": "A general, unspecified pardon is sufficient.", "reasons": "QURTUBI reports this view only to reject it, because the injured person might judge differently after learning the details."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q09", "question": "Why does the wording use these pronouns without repeating the sons as subject?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q09/p1", "position": "Each pronoun clearly points back to its own speaker, so the subject need not be repeated.", "reasons": "BIQAI says the pronoun references are plain from the context."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q10", "question": "Why is the admission to Jacob explicit and emphatic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q10/p1", "position": "They explicitly request forgiveness and use emphatic إنّا before Jacob, unlike their lighter إن and unnamed offense before Joseph.", "reasons": "SAMARRAI contrasts the brothers' speech to Joseph, where they neither asked him to forgive them nor named their offense, with their explicit plea and admission to their father; he also points to 12:98."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q11", "question": "What does the sons' confession signify for repentance and pardon?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q11/p1", "position": "It is a genuine admission of guilt and repentance, making forgiveness and intercession fitting.", "reasons": "BAGHAWI says they call themselves sinners. IBNATIYYA says they acknowledged wrongdoing even after Joseph's pardon. BAYDAWI says one who confesses sin is entitled to pardon and to ask forgiveness. BIQAI cites a Prophetic report that God accepts a servant who confesses and repents. ALUSI links admission to fitting pardon and intercession. ELMALILI stresses remorse; IBNASHUR calls the plea repentance; ISLAHI says they recognized their folly after events unfolded, as in their confession to Joseph at 12:91."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q12", "question": "What does 'khāṭiʾīn' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q12/p1", "position": "It means sinners or wrongdoers; the sin can fall short of shirk.", "reasons": "BAGHAWI and JISHUMI gloss the admission as calling themselves sinners. DAMGHANI says khāṭiʾūn can mean sinners whose sin is not shirk, and IBNJAWZI-NUZHA says khaṭaʾ can have that sense. BIQAI and BURSEVI specify deliberate wrongdoing. ZAJJAJ distinguishes khaṭiʾa/yakhṭaʾu from akhṭaʾa/yukhṭiʾu and cites an Imruʾ al-Qays line using khaṭiʾna."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q13", "question": "How is 'khāṭiʾīn' read in the canonical readings?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q13/p1", "position": "The ten canonical readings elide the hamza while preserving the root and meaning.", "reasons": "QIRAAT-ER gives this as the ten-reading form."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q14", "question": "What inward meaning does the family's gathering carry?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q14/p1", "position": "Gathering the family figures the gathering of all faculties into moderation under the heart's mediation.", "reasons": "QASHANI says the heart mediates between higher and lower faculties and restrains bodily pleasure-seeking."}]}
{"id": "12:97/q15", "question": "What does the wider Joseph story teach about how God directs events?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:97/q15/p1", "position": "God directs human affairs in ways people cannot foresee; they may dislike what is good or like what is bad for them.", "reasons": "ASAD contrasts this lesson of the Qur'anic story with Genesis' romantic account of Joseph's fortunes and cites 2:216."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q01", "question": "Who does “to Him” refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q01/p1", "position": "God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān identify the pronoun as God."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q02", "question": "What does daʿwah mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the noun is explained by ordinary usage or collective reference.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q02/p1", "position": "Calling or requesting the addressee to turn toward the caller, often for help or favor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes the core call from its religious use for deliverance or blessing, since literal turning toward God is impossible. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says request and fulfillment complete, but do not define, call and response."}, {"id": "13:14/q02/p2", "position": "A singular noun that can stand for the supplications of many callers.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī prefers Abū Bakr's reading; callers properly ask the One able to answer, grant and not disappoint."}]}

{"id": "13:14/q04", "question": "How does the genitive construction “call of truth” work?", "turns_on": "Whether the two nouns denote one qualified thing or a relation between the call and its object or origin.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q04/p1", "position": "It joins two expressions for the same true invocation, or a noun with its qualifying truth.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Jishumī compare دار الآخرة in 12:109; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Wāḥidī say the nouns differ in form; Ibn al-Jawzī says they name one reality. {"id": "13:14/q05", "question": "How does the opening reserve true invocation for God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q05/p1", "position": "The fronted “to Him” conveys entitlement and exclusivity, reinforced by the denial of any response from other gods.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the lām figurative possession by right; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes preposing and the next clause. {"id": "13:14/q06", "question": "What inward call of truth and false call are described?", "turns_on": "Whether inward response is described as illumination through truth or annihilation of self and orientation to the Essence.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q06/p1", "position": "Truth summons by or toward God and illuminates the responsive heart; ego and Satan draw it toward error.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says answering truth brings one to God, whereas ego brings ruin; Junayd excludes ego and Satan and describes lights without doubt. Al-Qushayrī contrasts proof heard with understanding and heedless obedience to satanic and self-interested promptings."}, {"id": "13:14/q06/p2", "position": "The answered call belongs to one annihilated from self and abiding in God, while selfhood or attachment to divine names veils response.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī connects pure religion to 39:3 and distinguishes God's Essence from names and attributes; self-standing petitioners address imagined objects."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q07", "question": "Who are “those who call besides Him” or “those called”?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative refers to the invoked objects or their callers, and whether those objects are only idols or include rational beings.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q07/p1", "position": "The relative phrase denotes idols or false gods invoked by polytheists; the callers and an object or resumptive pronoun are understood.", "reasons": "Most commentators identify idols, including al-Wāḥidī's “all interpreters.” Ibn ʿĀshūr makes idolaters the subject of يدعون and omits its object pronoun; al-Bayḍāwī gives both grammatical routes. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says informed devotees recognize such beings behind idols, yet none controls life, death, benefit or harm."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q08", "question": "What does “apart from Him” mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q08/p1", "position": "Other than, apart from, or away from God.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda compares dūnahu with ʿanhu and cites a poet's dūnī; al-Ṭabarī cites usage for falling short of someone. {"id": "13:14/q09", "question": "How is “they call” read and whom does it address?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is the usual third-person report or a transmitted direct address.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q09/p1", "position": "A reported second-person تدعون directly addresses the callers.", "reasons": "Al-Yazīdī transmits it from Abū ʿAmr; al-Samīn says it supports the alternative parsing. {"id": "13:14/q10", "question": "Why are invoked idols described with rational plural forms?", "turns_on": "Whether grammatical rationality reflects worshippers' treatment of idols or the mixed referents themselves.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q10/p1", "position": "The worshippers treat idols as rational agents, so the text follows their conception.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī points to 7:195; al-Samīn also allows that the set of worshipped beings includes both rational and inanimate objects. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this conventional Arab usage."}, {"id": "13:14/q10/p2", "position": "The forms naturally cover rational beings worshipped alongside inanimate idols.", "reasons": "Elmālılı argues the apparent relative wording includes rational beings and so cannot be limited to idols."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q11", "question": "What do istijābah and “they answer” mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the question asks the verb's lexical sense or the incapacity it asserts here.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q11/p1", "position": "The idols cannot hear, answer, grant benefit, avert harm, or give even a minimal response.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls the idols deficient; several explain that inert stone or images cannot perceive a plea. Ibn ʿĀshūr says bāʾ plus indefinite شيء denies even a promise or excuse; the Study Quran cites 5:76, 10:18, 25:55, 35:13, 7:194, 31:29, 34:22 and Last Day passages 18:52 and 28:64."}, {"id": "13:14/q11/p2", "position": "Responding to a caller or following the requested action.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī cite poetry for “answer”; Biqāʿī emphasizes compliance with the caller's will. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the augmented form intensifies answering; Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī note a shade of seeking in istijābah."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q12", "question": "Can creatures answer a plea independently of God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q12/p1", "position": "No creature has independent power to hear, affect, create, or answer; all interaction depends on God's will.", "reasons": "Elmālılı notes that ordinary public cries can be heard, rejects a forced restriction to inward prayer, and argues that separate beings cannot connect by themselves. He cites clouds, lightning, Zayd and ʿAmr, breath and physicians, 2:186, and God's power to bring water to the thirsty. People and angels respond only by His leave. Ṭabāṭabāʾī grounds the denial in God's sole dominion; Kuran Yolu contrasts Creator and created."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q13", "question": "What is the force of “with anything”?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q13/p1", "position": "It denies the smallest answer, even a verbal promise or excuse, much less fulfillment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says bāʾ marks what one answers with, unlike outcome fulfillment without it at 12:34; the indefinite شيء belittles any imaginable reply."}]}

{"id": "13:14/q15", "question": "What situation does the water image depict?", "turns_on": "Whether the hands gesture from afar, reach down a well, remain open in water, pursue a reflection, or belong to the Cain report.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q15/p1", "position": "A thirsty person calls or gestures to distant, insensible water, hoping it will move to his mouth; it never does.", "reasons": "Mujāhid repeatedly specifies tongue and hand. Al-Zajjāj says this and the well image have the same outcome; Jishumī reports the judge favors it. Al-Ālūsī sees urgent need and mockery in the composite comparison; water cannot perceive gestures, just as idols cannot hear. Biqāʿī says إلى shows the hands do not reach water."}, {"id": "13:14/q15/p2", "position": "Someone stretches open fingers into or toward water to scoop it, but cannot retain or carry it to the mouth.", "reasons": "Qatāda and al-Ḍaḥḥāk stress hands remaining spread; Ibn Qutayba says an implicit scooping action is understood. Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba invoke an Arab proverb for pursuing the unattainable, supported by poems of Ḍābiʾ and others on lost love. Al-Ālūsī distinguishes open باسط from closing a hand; Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the open-handed failed scoop. Al-ʿAwfī's Ibn ʿAbbās says hands already in water cannot lift it."}, {"id": "13:14/q15/p3", "position": "A thirsty person at the edge of a well reaches down without a rope or bucket; its water cannot rise to him.", "reasons": "ʿAlī, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Farrāʾ supply the well or lack of drawing equipment. Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī say “water” stands for its source, supported by a poem about a dug well. Al-Wāḥidī distinguishes reaching without a means from calling distant water; al-Ālūsī says it returns to the first explanation."}, {"id": "13:14/q15/p4", "position": "A thirsty person sees his reflection in distant water and mistakes it for reachable help.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is transmitted through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa and Ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, as well as other reports; al-Māwardī says the impression deceives him."}, {"id": "13:14/q15/p5", "position": "A person reaches toward water from a distance and dies before attaining it.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī puts the water below and far away; al-Ḥasan says death precedes reaching it. Qatāda says the neck tears from thirst; Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī stress death without benefit."}, {"id": "13:14/q15/p6", "position": "Cain is suspended over the sea, feeling the water yet unable to reach it.", "reasons": "Bukayr ibn Maʿrūf's report adds summer heat and winter snow. Al-Ālūsī rejects the report as unreliable."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q16", "question": "What kind of comparison is the water image?", "turns_on": "Whether the likeness is analyzed as a whole scene, a proverbial futile act, or its moral outcome.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q16/p1", "position": "An individual proverb for futile pursuit, comparable to writing on water.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba cite Arab usage and poems on grasped water; al-Ālūsī reports and challenges the claim that a meager result is obtained, saying the result is none."}, {"id": "13:14/q16/p2", "position": "A compound scene of urgent need, failed action, and insensible object, depicting utter failure of idols to respond.", "reasons": "Al-Rummānī combines need, grief and the warning to pray only to God; Būrsawī names a multiple-part parable. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the exception spans caller, object, call and response and works ironically; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it only appears to be a response."}, {"id": "13:14/q16/p3", "position": "The image warns that devotion to a powerless god gives neither benefit nor protection, through life or after death.", "reasons": "Qatāda says the worshipper dies in the practice; Ibn Kathīr explicitly extends the loss to this life and the next; Islahi calls the false gods self-appointed deities and intercessors, a mirage."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q17", "question": "How is bāsiṭ read?", "turns_on": "Whether the participle is annexed or carries nunation.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q17/p1", "position": "A reported reading gives bāsiṭ tanwīn: “like a spreader of his two palms.”", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says it makes the person generic; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān also report it."}, {"id": "13:14/q17/p2", "position": "The usual reading annexes bāsiṭ to “his two palms.”", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says its ordinary sense is spreading the fingers, not clasping them; an anonymous line supports the open hand."}]}
{"id": "13:14/q18", "question": "What do kaff and the two palms denote?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q18/p1", "position": "The two open palms or gripping parts of the hands.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān gives akuff and kufūf as its plurals and treats its root as a verbal noun; Biqāʿī links the name to gathering fingertips. {"id": "13:14/q19", "question": "What can a right-hand image imply in Arabic poetry?", "turns_on": "Whether the poem's context is generosity and agency or physical combat.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q19/p1", "position": "It can signify deliberate care, entrusted action, and generous purpose.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī reads al-Shammākh's banner as ʿArāba's generosity in supplying the poet; al-Buḥturī's hand in a patron's right hand indicates agency and names Yūnus ibn Bughā. {"id": "13:14/q37", "question": "How does Qur'anic expression use parables and concision?", "turns_on": "Whether the discussion concerns constructed parables or the broader economy and variety of Qur'anic expression.", "positions": [{"id": "13:14/q37/p1", "position": "It develops symbolic scenes into explicit, inventive parables, including the futile water-seeker.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts forgotten settings of Arab proverbs with Qur'anic scenes and lists storm-driven ash at 14:18, a falling associator at 22:31 and a mirage at 24:39–40."}, {"id": "13:14/q37/p2", "position": "Its varied sura styles and concise wording allow layered meanings and contextually signaled ellipsis.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts ceremonial openings (1:1, 2:1–2) and direct openings (47:1, 9:1); cites compressed teachings in 24:52, 28:7, 2:179; omissions in 2:177 and 26:63; general-for-particular statements; and al-Zamakhsharī on abbreviation at 74:1. {"id": "13:15/q02", "question": "Who are those in the heavens and earth?", "turns_on": "The scope of من and whether it is literal, predominant, or inward.", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q02/p1", "position": "Angels above and morally responsible humans or jinn below.", "reasons": "Muqatil names angels and believers; Tabrisī includes accountable creatures; Bursevi adds higher spirits, saints, prophets, earthly angels, and believing jinn; Elmalili names humans and jinn."}, {"id": "13:15/q02/p2", "position": "Every created thing, using a rational pronoun by predominance or extension.", "reasons": "Biqai includes animate and inanimate, rational and irrational; Asad cites shadows and 16:48–49, 22:18; Tabatabai reports but rejects the predominance explanation."}, {"id": "13:15/q02/p3", "position": "Rational beings are central; their prostration implies that of other creatures.", "reasons": "Alusi centers angels, humans, and jinn; Tabatabai says this addresses polytheists; Samarrai says willingness suits rational من; Ibn Ashur calls the generality conventional, a great multitude."}, {"id": "13:15/q02/p4", "position": "They may signify spiritual realities above and lower souls below.", "reasons": "Elmalili gives intellects, spirits, higher faculties and lower souls; Qashani takes heavenly and earthly beings as spiritual realities with shadow forms."}]}

{"id": "13:15/q11", "question": "What does الغدو mean and what form is it?", "turns_on": "Plural noun or verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q11/p1", "position": "It denotes early mornings and is a plural of ghadāh or ghudwah.", "reasons": "Baydawi compares qanā from qanāh; Biqai means the day's first part; Ibn Ashur connects it to going out for needs; Qurtubi cites its pairing with plural āṣāl."}, {"id": "13:15/q11/p2", "position": "It is a verbal noun denoting morning or morning's time.", "reasons": "Akhfash says its form is verbal; Ibn Ashur allows an omitted 'time of'; Qurtubi offers this too. Akhfash compares ibkār from abkara and rejects deriving abkār from bakr because it is a verbal noun and faʿla does not normally pluralize as afʿāl."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q12", "question": "What does الآصال mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q12/p1", "position": "Late afternoons or evenings, from ʿaṣr to sunset; plural of aṣīl directly or through aṣl.", "reasons": "Majaz cites Abu Dhu'ayb and al-Nabigha; Tabari, Thalabi and others give aṣl and poetic aṣāʾil; Jishumi calls it evening's beginning; Biqai notes occasional midday use and night arising from aṣīl; Ibn Ashur mentions yellow sun. Bahr al-Ulum starts at zenith, al-Kawashi at ʿaṣr."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q13", "question": "What is the reading والإيصال?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q13/p1", "position": "Abu Mujliz reads al-īṣāl, a verbal noun for entering late afternoon.", "reasons": "Tabrisi calls it noncanonical; Ibn Jinni, quoted by Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi, compares the verb for entering morning; Alusi notes kasra on hamza."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q14", "question": "What further word associations does Biqai draw around āṣāl?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q14/p1", "position": "He explores joining and similar sounding roots, ending with aṣīl as an evening link or end.", "reasons": "Biqai derives ṣalā and prayer from connecting servant and Lord by supplication, mercy, praise, pardon, or ritual, and notes bodily hindquarters and the following racehorse. He traces ṣāl to pursuit or attack and waṣl to union, using joints, relatives, ewe offspring, garments, yarn, land and adjoining months. Roasting and heating join meat or hands to fire; ṣalāya is forehead or perfume pounder through repeated contact. A hadith supplies maṣālī for Satan's snares; Qazzaz explains the ṣilyān pasture plant and accusation forms. Similar forms name a snake, camel assault and continuous neigh. Aṣīl also means lineage; aṣl is foundation; al-aṣī is evening, night, day's end, even death. He refers to 11:87."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q15", "question": "Why mention morning and evening?", "turns_on": "Permanence or visible shadow behavior.", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q15/p1", "position": "They signify continual submission.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Qashani, Bursevi, Alusi and Study Quran infer permanence; Ibn Ashur says dawn-going and evening span shadow times."}, {"id": "13:15/q15/p2", "position": "Shadows are longest or most numerous then, and their motion most visible.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi give length and abundance; Tabatabai contrasts midday diminishment or absence (20:130); Asad and Kuranyolu describe daily changes."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q16", "question": "What does the time phrase modify?", "turns_on": "The whole prostration or shadows specifically.", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q16/p1", "position": "It modifies يسجد, with ب meaning في.", "reasons": "Samin and Bursevi treat the periods as prostration time; Alusi allows an implicit سجود."}, {"id": "13:15/q16/p2", "position": "It may describe the shadows' especially visible movement.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Alusi allow this attachment."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q17", "question": "What other Qur'anic passages explain this verse?", "turns_on": "The passage used as interpretive parallel.", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q17/p1", "position": "16:48–49 and related prostration passages explain shadows and creation's submission.", "reasons": "Tabari, Ibn Abbas through Thalabi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, Tabatabai, Kuranyolu and Study Quran cite 16:48; Study Quran adds 16:49 and 22:18; Samarrai contrasts 22:18's repeated من."}, {"id": "13:15/q17/p2", "position": "2:116 and 3:83 parallel universal obedience and willing or unwilling surrender.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites 3:83; Wahidi and Razi cite both; Study Quran invokes 2:116 and 3:83."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q18", "question": "How does the verse serve its context?", "turns_on": "Idolatry rebuke, call by decree, word order, or broader natural signs.", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q18/p1", "position": "It rebukes idolatry by showing all beings, including alleged deities, subject to God.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya offers display of power or rebuke of Quraysh and says Tabari favors rebuke; Abu Hayyan and Alusi stress idols lack power to help or harm; Ibn Ashur links 13:14's true invocation; Islahi calls rival calls a mirage and sees every object witnessing oneness; Tabatabai says the rational wording and shadows confront polytheists."}, {"id": "13:15/q18/p2", "position": "It follows the call by command with a call by decree.", "reasons": "Biqai connects the books and universal submission to 11:119; he describes the surah's aim as revelation's differing reception, like thunder, rain and lightning that benefit or harm depending on where they fall."}, {"id": "13:15/q18/p3", "position": "The order willing then unwilling guides benefit before harm in 13:16.", "reasons": "Samarrai reports this and contrasts Saba 34:39."}, {"id": "13:15/q18/p4", "position": "The surah's natural wonders show dependence on and glorification of God.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 13:12–13; Islahi calls the shadow image insinuative reasoning through human nature."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q19", "question": "What did Rabiʿ ibn Khuthaym say or do on reciting this verse?", "turns_on": "The different words reported.", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q19/p1", "position": "He affirmed it reverently: 'Indeed, my Lord.'", "reasons": "Tabari reports this response."}, {"id": "13:15/q19/p2", "position": "He prayed to be one who prostrates willingly.", "reasons": "Thalabi transmits through Ibn al-Mubarak and Sufyan; Durr situates the prayer at Surat al-Ra'd's prostration."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q20", "question": "What further inward lesson is drawn from voluntary submission?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q20/p1", "position": "The lover values service beyond Paradise and may be led there in golden chains.", "reasons": "Bursevi says devoted lovers refuse Paradise to continue serving; Khujandi's poem devalues the garden for a lover. A hadith describes people led to Paradise in chains."}]}
{"id": "13:15/q21", "question": "Was Surat al-Ra'd wholly revealed in Mecca?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:15/q21/p1", "position": "It was wholly Makkan, with no Madinan verse.", "reasons": "Islahi rejects the codices' Madinan classification."}]}
